titre: A vinyl curtain cuts a lake in two to isolate the role of phosphorus
accroche: In 1973, Canadian researchers split a lake in two and pour in the same nutrients, except one. Only one half turns green.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the early 1970s, a question of water chemistry delays legislation. Should phosphorus be removed from laundry detergents and wastewater to save lakes from the algal bloom that chokes them? Or is the real lever carbon, or nitrogen? Canada had already banned, since January 1, 1973, the sale of detergents with more than 2.2% phosphorus. In early 1974, in the American Great Lakes basin, only three states had followed: Indiana, New York, and Michigan. David Schindler, of the Freshwater Institute in Winnipeg, attributes a good part of this slowness to the controversy and confusion surrounding the debate.

## A proof at first too small

Schindler works in the Experimental Lakes Area, in northwestern Ontario, on lakes sitting on the Precambrian shield. First test: Lake 227, very poor in dissolved inorganic carbon, on the order of 2 to 3% of what is measured in the lower Great Lakes. If carbon limited the algae, this lake could not turn green. Phosphate and nitrate are poured in. Within a few weeks, it becomes a teeming green soup: more than 100 micrograms of chlorophyll a per liter are common, against 1 to 5 in neighboring unfertilized lakes. A lack of carbon therefore does not keep the lake from blooming.

The opposite objection remains: without phosphorus, would the bloom happen anyway? Trials in enclosures of 2 to 3 cubic meters, in the same lake, said no, but Schindler cites them as data then unpublished. What remained was to verify it on a whole lake.

## The curtain

Lake 226 has two similar basins, separated by a shallow neck. In 1973, the team stretches across it a vinyl curtain reinforced with nylon, 60 meters by 6, sealed into the sediments and fastened to the rock in the narrow passage. From the end of May, each basin receives the same nitrogen (as nitrate) and the same carbon (as sucrose), in twenty equal weekly additions. Only one also receives phosphorus: 0.59 gram per square meter per year, a dose that Schindler does not consider exceptional for a lake affected by human activity.

The two halves belong to the same lake, the same climate, the same year. A single variable changes.

On September 4, 1973, the photograph is taken. The phosphorus basin is covered with a bloom of the cyanobacterium *Anabaena spiroides*. The other basin, all year, keeps the plankton from before the experiment, mostly diatoms.

## What this says, and what it does not say

Another lake, Lake 304, had received phosphorus, nitrogen, and carbon in 1971 and 1972, and had bloomed. In 1973, the phosphorus alone is stopped: the lake recovers almost completely. Schindler draws a practical consequence. Banning or sharply reducing phosphates in laundry detergents could remove half of the phosphorus reaching the St. Lawrence Great Lakes, and could rapidly bring partial recovery of Lakes Erie and Ontario, as much as about ten years before control of phosphorus by other means becomes possible on a large scale.

The scope is that of a limiting nutrient, not a universal rule. Schindler compares his lakes with more than half of the waters that feed the Great Lakes. The experiment does not say that only phosphorus matters: nitrogen and carbon were present on both sides. It says that, in these waters, it was what was lacking, and therefore what was in command.

A 60-meter curtain had been enough to make visible at a glance what the debate had struggled to establish.

repere.texte: On September 4, 1973, the basin of Lake 226 fertilized with phosphorus, nitrogen, and carbon is covered with a bloom of Anabaena spiroides. The neighboring basin, which received the same amounts of nitrogen and carbon without phosphorus, remains at pre-fertilization conditions.
repere.source: D. W. Schindler, “Eutrophication and Recovery in Experimental Lakes: Implications for Lake Management,” Science 184 (4139), May 24, 1974, pp. 897–899

carte.punch: A vinyl curtain cut a lake in two. Only the half that received phosphorus turned green.
carte.idee: In 1973, Schindler splits Lake 226 into two basins with a 60-meter curtain. Both receive the same nitrogen and carbon; only one receives phosphorus. On September 4, only that one is covered with algae.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: History of the research site, headed by Schindler from 1968 to 1989 according to this article.

quiz.question: What does the contrast between the two halves of Lake 226 prove?
choix: That nitrogen and carbon suffice to make a lake bloom, even without phosphorus
That carbon, more abundant on the green side, is the nutrient that limits algae
That, with nitrogen and carbon already present on both sides, it was the missing phosphorus that limited the algae
That nitrogen is useless to the algae of a lake in the region
quiz.explication: The two basins received the same nitrogen and carbon, and only the phosphorus differed: it was what was lacking and what limited algal growth. Nitrogen is not useless: algae need it, but it was already present in sufficient quantity on both sides, so it does not explain the difference. Nor does the experiment show that phosphorus acts alone, since nitrogen and carbon were there on both sides, and Lake 227 had already ruled out carbon.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the team isolate phosphorus as the only variable between the two basins of Lake 226?
choix: By stretching a 60-meter vinyl curtain, sealed into the sediments, between the two basins
By completely draining one of the two basins for the whole duration of the experiment
By moving all the fish from one basin to the other every week
By filtering all the water of just one basin to remove its natural phosphorus
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A vinyl curtain reinforced with nylon, 60 meters by 6, sealed into the sediments, separates the two similar basins of Lake 226; both receive the same nitrogen and carbon, and only one also receives phosphorus.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens at Lake 304 when, in 1973, the phosphorus inputs alone are stopped?
choix: The lake keeps blooming at the same rate as before the stop
The lake immediately becomes poorer in nitrogen and carbon
The lake, which had bloomed in 1971 and 1972, recovers almost completely
The lake freezes unusually early the following winter
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lake 304 had received phosphorus, nitrogen, and carbon in 1971 and 1972 and had bloomed; in 1973, stopping the phosphorus alone was enough to bring about an almost complete recovery.
